episodes.title: Time, Compressed
episodes.subject: Time
episodes.hook: We have saved more time than any generation in history. So why does every one of us feel like we are running out of it?
episodes.question: Did you know that time itself has been compressing for five hundred years?
episodes.guess: Where did all the time we saved actually go? Write your guess in the comments before you press play.
episodes.summary: Seven centuries, seven mornings: from a village that wakes at midnight to a phone checked before your feet touch the floor — and what the year 2100 is about to take next.

quiz.question: Did time really speed up over 500 years?
options: No — we pack more into it and remember less
quiz.reveal: A second in 1500 lasted exactly as long as one today. What changed is how much we pack into it — and how little we remember.

questions.question: In 1500, how did many people sleep?
options: In two parts: a “first sleep” and a “second sleep”
Only in the afternoon, after lunch
Never more than four hours a night
Sitting up, so they would wake at dawn
questions.reveal: Historians have found hundreds of references to a “first sleep” and a “second sleep”. In between, people prayed, talked — even visited neighbours.

questions.question: What were England’s first coffeehouses nicknamed?
questions.reveal: For one penny you could walk in, read the news and argue with strangers for hours — London’s first coffeehouse opened in 1652.

questions.question: Workers in the 1700s often took one day off that was not Sunday. What did they call it?
questions.reveal: For generations, workers simply took Mondays off — “Saint Monday”. Factory clocks slowly made it disappear.

questions.question: How did the weekend begin?
options: With a free Friday for farmers
With half a Saturday: mill work ended at 2 p.m.
With a week off every summer
questions.reveal: An 1850 British law ended mill work for women and children at 2 p.m. on Saturdays. Soon the men got the same — even free time had to be written into law.

questions.question: On 18 November 1883, some American towns heard noon twice. Why?
options: The railroads switched to standard time zones
The Sun seemed to stop in the sky
A new law moved noon to 1 p.m.
questions.reveal: The railroads reset the clocks of a whole continent to standard time zones — the “Day of Two Noons”.

questions.question: What did Henry Ford offer his workers in 1914?
options: $5 a day for an eight-hour day
A free Model T every year
$1 a day for a twelve-hour day
questions.reveal: Ford more than doubled pay, to $5 a day, and cut the day to eight hours. By 1926 his workers had Saturdays off too.

questions.question: How long does the average internet user spend online every day?
questions.reveal: Adult internet users average 6 hours 38 minutes online — every single day.

questions.question: So where did all the time we saved go?
options: Clocks tick faster than they did in 1500
We pack more into every hour — and remember less of it
Days are shorter than they used to be
questions.reveal: A second in 1500 lasted exactly as long as one today. Your brain measures time with new memories — so hours that all look the same seem to vanish.

eras.line: It is midnight. Pitch black. And the whole village is awake.
eras.saw: Your day begins when the sun rises, and ends when it sets. The church bell is the only clock you will ever hear.

eras.line: The air smells of smoke — and of something new.
eras.saw: His drifts by seconds. For the first time, an ordinary day can be cut into minutes.

eras.line: Monday morning, and half the workshop is empty.
eras.saw: Time is now something you can carry. And something you can sell.

eras.line: At midday the church clock strikes twelve. Then it is noon again.
eras.saw: The railroads had reset the clocks of an entire continent.

eras.line: The line of people looking for work stretches down the street.
eras.saw: Henry Ford more than doubled his workers’ pay, to five dollars a day, and cut the day to eight hours.

eras.line: Before your feet touch the floor, you have already checked your phone.
eras.saw: On paper, we are the richest people in history, rich in time. And yet, ask anyone how they are, and you will hear the same word. Busy.

eras.line: That morning has not happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: It could finally arrive, a century late. But if history repeats, we will fill every freed hour with something faster.

facts.fact: For centuries, people slept twice a night. Historians have found hundreds of references to a “first sleep” and a “second sleep”.
facts.source: A. Roger Ekirch, At Day’s Close (2005)

facts.fact: England’s first coffeehouses were nicknamed “penny universities”: one penny bought coffee, the news and hours of argument with strangers.
For generations, workers simply took Mondays off. They called it “Saint Monday”.
The weekend began with half a Saturday: an 1850 British law ended mill work for women and children at 2 p.m. on Saturdays.
On 18 November 1883, American and Canadian railroads switched to standard time zones. Some towns heard noon twice that day — the “Day of Two Noons”.
facts.source: Chicago Public Library · The Day of Two Noons

facts.fact: Henry Ford more than doubled his workers’ pay, to $5 a day — and cut the working day to eight hours.
The average internet user now spends 6 hours 38 minutes online, every single day.

Your brain measures time with memories, not clocks. A week full of new experiences feels long when you look back; months of routine shrink to almost nothing. Psychologists call it the holiday paradox.

episodes.commentPrompt: If you could wake up in any century, from 1500 to 2100, which would you choose — and why?

episodes.title: The Sun
episodes.subject: The Sun
episodes.hook: Every time you look at the Sun, you are looking into the past.
episodes.question: Did you know that you have never once seen the Sun as it is right now?
episodes.guess: That light on your face is eight minutes old. But the energy inside it — how old is that? Guess in the comments, then stay to the end and check.
episodes.summary: Seven mornings under the same Sun, and one relationship that climbs rung by rung: Midsummer bonfires in Tudor London, the first telescope drawing of sunspots, leaves that bubble in sunlight, Herschel’s invisible light, the suntan myth, solar power almost eleven times bigger in ten years — and a 2100 scenario, clearly labelled, where the Sun might decide whether your AI wakes up.

quiz.question: How old is the sunlight hitting your eyes right now?
quiz.reveal: Sunlight needs about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross the average Earth–Sun distance — and the energy in it was made in the Sun’s core long before that (NASA estimates about 170,000 years). You have never seen the Sun as it is — only as it was.

questions.question: In 1500, what did almost everyone believe about the Sun?
options: That it goes around the Earth
That it is a bonfire in the sky
That it is made of iron
That it stands still at the centre
questions.reveal: It is what Ptolemy had taught, about 1,400 years earlier. In 1543, the year he died, Copernicus’s book put the Sun at the centre instead.

questions.question: Who made the first telescope drawing of sunspots?
options: Thomas Harriot, beside the River Thames
questions.reveal: On a misty December morning in 1610, the Englishman Thomas Harriot pointed a telescope at the low Sun and drew what he saw — and never published it. Galileo’s letters on the spots came out in 1613.

questions.question: In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz sank leaves under water. What did he see in sunlight?
options: They bubbled out fresh air — and stopped in the shade
questions.reveal: In more than 500 experiments he found that only the green parts do it, and only in light. Plants need the Sun.

questions.question: In 1800, William Herschel put thermometers in a rainbow made by a prism. Where was the hottest spot?
options: In the yellow, the brightest colour
Just past the red, where nothing was visible
questions.reveal: The reading beyond the red was the highest of all. Herschel had found infrared — the Sun was sending more than our eyes could catch.

questions.question: How leaves turn sunlight into sugar got its name in 1893. What is it called?
questions.reveal: The name is usually credited to the American botanist Charles Reid Barnes. Nearly all life runs on it — your lunch is stored sunlight.

questions.question: The famous story says Coco Chanel started the suntan craze. What did a historian find?
options: It is true — she returned tanned from a cruise in 1923
It is probably a myth, traced to an unsigned magazine article from 1971
It was actually her rival Elsa Schiaparelli
Tanning was banned in France until 1930
questions.reveal: Kerry Segrave traced the Chanel story to an unsigned 1971 magazine article; tanning was already a fad before 1920. The real reason was work: as jobs moved indoors, a tan became the badge of leisure.

questions.question: In 2025, how much electricity did solar power make compared with ten years earlier?
questions.reveal: About 2,770 TWh in 2025 against about 250 TWh in 2015 — almost nine percent of all the world’s electricity.

questions.question: So how old is the sunlight hitting your face right now?
options: About 8 minutes 20 seconds — and its energy left the Sun’s core long before that
questions.reveal: Light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross 150 million km. But the energy in it was made in the Sun’s core and spent a very long time struggling out — NASA estimates about 170,000 years. When it began its journey there were no farms, no cities and no writing.

eras.line: It is Midsummer Eve, and the streets are glowing with firelight.
eras.saw: It’s the difference between day and night. Daylight is for work. Darkness is for sleep, and prayer.

eras.line: A misty December morning. The Sun hangs low and dim — and a man points a telescope at it.
eras.saw: For a few people with telescopes, the Sun has become something to watch. Closely.

eras.line: A bright summer morning, and the fashionable ladies are hiding from the Sun under parasols.
eras.saw: This summer, the Sun is turning into something new. Something to explain.

eras.line: An astronomer has set a prism in a sunbeam, with thermometers whose bulbs are blackened.
eras.saw: Now the Sun is something you measure, even where your eyes give up.

eras.line: Hot sand. Salt air. And everyone is lying in the Sun, on purpose.
eras.saw: The Sun used to be something to measure. Now, it’s the source of every meal.

eras.line: Your phone’s charged, the lights come on — and a field of solar panels has been awake since sunrise.
eras.saw: So what’s the Sun to you now? Power. Something you harvest, like a crop.

eras.line: That morning has not happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: In 1500, the Sun decided when you went to sleep. In 2100, it might decide whether your AI wakes up.

facts.fact: In 1500, almost everyone believed the Sun goes around the Earth — what Ptolemy had taught about 1,400 years earlier. In 1543, the year he died, Copernicus’s book put the Sun at the centre.

The first telescope drawing of sunspots was made on 8 December 1610 by the Englishman Thomas Harriot, beside the Thames — not by Galileo, who published his letters on the spots in 1613. Harriot never published his.

In the summer of 1779, the Dutch doctor Jan Ingenhousz ran more than 500 experiments on plants. Leaves sunk in water bubbled out fresh air in sunlight and stopped in the shade — and only the green parts did it.
William Herschel set a prism in a sunbeam and found the hottest spot just past the red, where nothing was visible. He had found infrared: the Sun sends more than our eyes can catch.
Leaves catch sunlight and turn it into sugar, and nearly all life runs on that. The process got its name in 1893 — photosynthesis — usually credited to the American botanist Charles Reid Barnes.
The story that Coco Chanel started the suntan craze is probably a myth: a historian traced it to an unsigned 1971 magazine article. As work moved indoors, a tan became the badge of leisure.
facts.source: Kerry Segrave, Suntanning in 20th Century America (2005)

facts.fact: In 2025, solar power made almost eleven times more electricity than ten years earlier: about 2,770 TWh, against about 250 TWh in 2015. That is almost 9% of all the world’s electricity.

Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach you. But the energy in it was made in the Sun’s core and took a very long time to get out — NASA estimates about 170,000 years. You have never seen the Sun as it is. Only as it was.

episodes.commentPrompt: In which century would you rather watch the Sun rise?

episodes.title: School
episodes.subject: School
episodes.hook: Five hundred years ago, most children never saw a classroom. They worked.
episodes.question: Did you know that the word “school” first meant the one thing school seems to take away from you?
episodes.guess: Two hundred years ago, out of every ten people on Earth, how many could read? Guess in the comments, then stay to the end and check.
episodes.summary: Seven mornings, seven school days — or days with no school at all: a prince with his own tutor in Tudor London, a 1647 law that begins by blaming the devil, the Prussian law that banned school holidays, Joseph Lancaster’s thousand-pupil schools and their cages, the high-school boom and a right to education for everyone, the 2020 closures — and a 2100 scenario, clearly labelled, where every child might have a tutor.

quiz.question: Two hundred years ago, out of every ten people on Earth, how many could read?
quiz.reveal: About one in ten: historians estimate about 12% of the world could read in 1820. Today it is almost nine in ten — 87% of adults in 2022.

questions.question: In 1500, who taught nine-year-old Prince Henry, the future Henry VIII?
options: A village priest, with forty other boys
The poet John Skelton — a teacher all to himself
Nobody — princes did not learn to read
questions.reveal: One teacher, one child. Most children learned by working — a craftsman’s son was usually apprenticed for seven years — but a prince had the poet John Skelton all to himself.

questions.question: How does one of America’s first school laws, from Massachusetts in 1647, begin?
options: By thanking the King of England
With a list of fines for lazy pupils
questions.reveal: It calls keeping people from the Scriptures a chief project of “that old deluder, Satan”. Any town with fifty households had to hire someone to teach reading and writing.

questions.question: What did Frederick the Great’s 1763 school law in Prussia ban?
options: School holidays — not even at harvest time
questions.reveal: “No vacations are to be given, not even during harvest time.” Every boy and girl was to go from five until about thirteen — though plenty of families just ignored the rules.

questions.question: Joseph Lancaster claimed one master could run a school of how many children?
questions.reveal: His trick: older children taught the younger ones in small groups. Pupils wrote letters in sand because paper cost money — and a misbehaving child might be hoisted up in a cage.

questions.question: In 1880, school became compulsory in England. For which ages?
questions.reveal: From five to ten. Fees were still charged until 1891, when school became free for most families.

questions.question: In December 1948, in Paris, the United Nations wrote down for the whole world that everyone has the right to…
options: Education — free, at least in the early years
questions.reveal: Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: “Everyone has the right to education.” Free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages.

questions.question: In April 2020, about how many learners were sent home as schools closed?
options: About 1.6 billion — more than nine in ten students on Earth
questions.reveal: UNESCO counted more than 1.6 billion learners out of school at the peak, in over 190 countries. Lessons moved into kitchens and bedrooms.

questions.question: “School” comes from the ancient Greek word scholé. What did it first mean?
questions.reveal: In Athens, people with free time often spent it talking, arguing and learning — so the word for leisure became the word for learned talk, and then for the place you learn.

eras.line: It’s still dark. Next door, a hammer’s already going, and the street smells of wet straw and wood smoke.
eras.saw: Something for other people. For priests, and rich boys. Most children learn by working.

eras.line: There’s frost on the window, and the cows need milking before breakfast.
eras.saw: A way to read God’s word, with your own eyes.

eras.line: It’s autumn. The war’s just over, the harvest’s in, and the pastor has news from the king.
eras.saw: An order. From the king.

eras.line: One enormous hall. Hundreds of children, in long rows. And just one master.
eras.saw: A machine. For teaching the poor, by the hundred, as cheaply as possible.

eras.line: It’s June. Graduation day. Your mum’s ironing your gown, and the radio’s on.
eras.saw: So now school is a right. And a ladder. And a building you walk to every morning.

eras.line: Your phone buzzes. Homework’s due at midnight. And any question you’ve got, you can ask a screen.
eras.saw: Always on. A classroom, plus a screen that never closes.

eras.line: That morning hasn’t happened yet. But we can follow the evidence.
eras.saw: In 1500, a private teacher was for a prince. In 2100, it might be for everyone.

facts.fact: In 1500, nine-year-old Prince Henry — the future Henry VIII — had a teacher all to himself: the poet John Skelton. Most children learned by working, and historians estimate only about one woman in a hundred in England could even write her own name.
facts.source: EBSCO · Luminarium (Skelton) · David Cressy, Literacy and the Social Order (1980)

facts.fact: One of America’s first school laws, Massachusetts 1647, begins by blaming “that old deluder, Satan”. Any town with fifty households had to hire someone to teach reading and writing; a hundred households, a grammar school too — or the town paid a fine.
facts.source: Massachusetts Archives · Records of the Massachusetts Bay (1853)

facts.fact: Frederick the Great’s 1763 school law banned school holidays — “not even during harvest time”. Every boy and girl was to go from five until about thirteen, and parents of children who skipped could be fined.

Joseph Lancaster claimed one master could run a school of more than a thousand children, with older pupils teaching the younger ones. Misbehave, and you might be hoisted above the classroom in a cage — he thought it beat the cane.
facts.source: Joseph Lancaster, Improvements in Education (1803) · Dictionary of Canadian Biography

facts.fact: In 1880, school became compulsory in England for children from five to ten. Fees were still charged until 1891, when school became free for most families.
facts.source: UK Parliament, Living Heritage: the 1870 Education Act

facts.fact: On 10 December 1948, in Paris, the United Nations wrote it down for the whole world: “Everyone has the right to education.” Free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages.
facts.source: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 26

facts.fact: In April 2020, about 1.6 billion learners were sent home as schools closed — more than nine in ten students on Earth. At least 463 million children could not get remote lessons at all.
facts.source: UNESCO COVID-19 education monitoring (2020) · UNICEF, Remote Learning Reachability (2020)

facts.fact: “School” comes from the ancient Greek scholé, which meant free time — leisure. In Athens, people with free time often spent it in discussion, so the word for leisure became the word for the place you learn. And literacy? About one in ten could read in 1820; today it is almost nine in ten.
facts.source: Liddell–Scott–Jones Greek Lexicon · Our World in Data, Literacy
